qs.q: What is the approximate percentage of primary lung tumours that are carcinomas?
qs.e: Approximately 95% of primary lung tumours are carcinomas, while the remaining 5% comprise carcinoids, mesenchymal malignancies, lymphomas, and benign lesions. The 5% option represents the minority of non-carcinoma lung tumours rather than the carcinomas.
qs.s: Lung Tumours Conti — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is identified as the most common benign lung tumour presenting as a discrete coin lesion on imaging?
o: Hamartoma
Fibrosarcoma
Leiomyoma
Bronchial carcinoid
qs.e: Hamartoma is the most common benign lung tumour, typically appearing as a spherical, small coin lesion composed mainly of mature cartilage, fat, fibrous tissue, and blood vessels. Fibrosarcoma and leiomyoma are mesenchymal malignancies rather than the most common benign lesion.
qs.s: Lung Tumours Conti — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung tumour. Which population is most characteristically associated?
o: Male patients with a long history of heavy cigarette smoking.
Individuals employed in uranium mining occupations.
Workers with documented exposure to asbestos fibers.
Women and individuals who have never smoked cigarettes.
qs.e: Adenocarcinoma is the most common primary lung cancer in non-smokers and women, and is often located peripherally.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - March 7, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Adenocarcinoma has become the most common primary lung tumour. Which population is most characteristically affected?
o: Elderly males with a documented history of occupational asbestos exposure
Women, non-smokers, and individuals under the age of forty-five years
Middle-aged males with greater than forty pack-year smoking history
Immunocompromised patients suffering from recurrent pulmonary infections
qs.e: Adenocarcinoma is now the most common lung cancer overall, particularly in women, non-smokers, and those under 45 — a demographic shift from squamous cell carcinoma.

qs.q: The neuroendocrine spectrum of lung tumours ordered from lowest to highest malignant potential is
o: Typical carcinoid → atypical carcinoid → large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma → SCLC
Atypical carcinoid → typical carcinoid → SCLC → large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma → atypical carcinoid → typical carcinoid → SCLC
SCLC → large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma → atypical carcinoid → typical carcinoid
qs.e: The correct spectrum of increasing aggressiveness is: typical carcinoid → atypical carcinoid → large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma → SCLC.

qs.q: Ectopic ACTH syndrome from a lung tumour characteristically shows
o: Very high cortisol + very high ACTH + hypokalaemic alkalosis, NOT suppressed by high-dose DST
Low cortisol, low ACTH, hyperkalaemia
Cortisol suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone
Low cortisol, high ACTH, hypernatraemia
qs.e: Ectopic ACTH: very high ACTH → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia → very high cortisol, hypokalaemia (mineralocorticoid effect), metabolic alkalosis. Does NOT suppress with high-dose dexamethasone — distinguishing it from pituitary Cushing's disease.
